name: Toda
catalog_citation: Emeneau, Murray B. 1957 [issued 1958]. Toda, a Dravidian language. Transactions of the Philological Society 1957: 15-66; read in the author's reprint: Emeneau, M. B. 1967. Dravidian Linguistics, Ethnology and Folktales: Collected Papers (Annamalai University,…
catalog_locator: Emeneau 1957 sec. 19, TPS p. 25 = 1967 reprint p. 8; page image the copy we hold (archive.org item tdl.18199-dravidian-linguistics-ethnology-and-folktales-coll…
catalog_quote: § 19. Accent and intonation patterns must in general be ignored here. One of the intonation patterns is interesting however—perhaps even peculiar to Toda among all the Dravidian languages—and may be mentioned. Words are accompanied on the first syllable by primary stress, secondary stress, or weak stress. In sentences that are statements or are questions containing an interrogative word, the intonation pattern consists of a slight drop in pitch on the syllable or syllables following the last primary stress, or alternatively, a whispering of these syllables. Frequently the whispering starts back of the last primary stress, and sometimes the whole sentence is whispered.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: 1.4. Accent. Isolated words have stress on the first or only syllable - the stress is audible, though not so strong as that of English. Within phrases the strongest stress is usually on the first word, and successive words have a weaker stress. Whether three levels are to be recognized - strong, weaker, weakest could not be determined accurately, but there was some suspicion that such was the case. If it is, the placing of the varying stresses presumably depends on rules concerning immediate constituencies, and is a subject for further research. No contrasts were found depending on stress levels or positions.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the first syllable (the only syllable in monosyllables); it is non-contrastive and phonetically moderate. Emeneau's earlier sketch (TPS 1957: 24-25) says the same: 'Words are accompanied on the first syllable by primary stress, secondary stress, or weak stress', the level being set by position in the phrase.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No word-internal secondary stress described. Gradation is between words: in a phrase the first word carries the strongest stress and following words weaker stress; possibly three levels (strong/weaker/weakest), undetermined; 1957 version labels these primary/secondary/weak stress, always on the word's first syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: None; 'No contrasts were found depending on stress levels or positions.' (LSI Tamil Nadu 2023 p.660 gives a muddled alternative -- initial unless /a/-conditioned shift, 'barely perceptible', or penultimate -- prefaced by 'The matter of stress is not quite clear'; not adopted here.)
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is explicitly for isolated (citation-form) words; phrase level: strongest stress on the phrase-initial word; sentence level (sec. 1.5): pitch drop and/or whispering of syllables after the last strong stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Toda proper (toda1252, ISO tcx), Nilgiri Hills, Tamil Nadu; Emeneau's data are from his 1935-38 fieldwork. No dialect split is relevant to the stress statement. The LSI Tamil Nadu 2023 Toda chapter (fieldwork Dec 2021-Jan 2022) is nominally the same language but contains boilerplate apparently carried over from other chapters, so its stress section should not be treated as an independent description.

Words are accompanied on the first syllable by primary stress, secondary stress, or weak stress. In sentences that are statements or are questions containing an interrogative word, the intonation pattern consists of a slight drop in pitch on the syllable or syllables following the last primary stress, or alternatively, a whispering of these syllables.'); the bracketed [26] page break falls lower in sec. 20, so reprint p. 8 = TPS p. 25 is right. The continuation (whispering may start further back; example 'he has really come' with last two syllables whispered) is sentence i…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (initial) and as the existing Emeneau 1984 sec. 1.4 statement; this is the earlier (1957) formulation of the same author's claim, adding the three-degree stress grading and the sentence-final pitch drop/whispering.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every word carries its stress on the first syllable; what varies between words is only the degree of that initial stress (primary, secondary or weak), which is a phrase-level matter. Sentence intonation is a pitch drop or whispering after the last primary stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Three degrees of stress are named (primary, secondary, weak) but all fall on the first syllable of a word; no secondary stress within a word on a non-initial syllable is described.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the author says accent 'must in general be ignored here', so the statement is brief.
new_statements.identity_note: Emeneau's 1957 paper describes the Toda of the Nilgiri Hills from his own 1935-38 fieldwork; no dialect is distinguished. The other works do not describe a distinct variety. The Krishnamurti item on archive.org is an ERIC microfiche card, not the book.

readall_conflicts: Among the listed works there is no disagreement: Emeneau 1957/1967 (initial, three degrees) agrees with the catalog and with Emeneau 1984 sec. 1.4; Krishnamurti 2003 and Sakthivel 1977 are silent; Shalev et al. 1993 could not be opened. One source outside the works list, already held by the project from our earlier reading, does disagree with itself: the Linguistic Survey of India: Tamil Nadu (2023) chapter 'Toda' (S. Banerjee), sec. 2.8.4 'Stress', p. 660, says 'The matter of stress is not quite clear' and lists (a) stress on the first syllable except when it lacks /a/ and the second syllable has it, (b) stress barely perceptible, (c) stress typically on the penultimate syllable, shifting left when the penult vowel is schwa. Its (c) contradicts the initial-stress reading; the chapter gives no examples for any of the three and the rest of its phonology section (e.g. /ghər/ 'house') looks like non-Toda material, so it is not treated as evidence against Emeneau.

sources.note: Verbatim p.660: 'The matter of stress is not quite clear (a) Stress is on the first syllable except when it doesn't have /a/ and the second syllable does. (b) Stress is barely perceptible. (c) Stress typically falls on the penultimate syllable of a word, however, if the penultimate vowel in a word with more than two syllables is schwa, stress falls on the preceding syllable.' Internally contradictory; chapter shows boilerplate carried over from other LSI chapters (e.g. morphology example /ghər/ 'house' is not Toda), so low evidential weight.
